She was so absorbed in admiring those gentle blue eyes, in conversing and listening, and devising all the little schemes that lay between, that the evening passed with an unusually swift haste; and the supper table, which always concluded such gatherings and at which she had been accustomed to sit and watch the appointed hour, was already laid out and ready, and had been moved nearer the fire before she even noticed. With a promptness beyond the ordinary impulse of a spirit that had never been indifferent to the merit of doing everything well and attentively, and with the genuine goodwill of a mind delighted by its own ideas, she then performed all the honours of the meal, presenting and praising the minced chicken and the scalloped oysters with a zeal she knew would suit the early hour and the genteel sensibilities of their guests.

On such occasions poor Mr. Woodhouse found his feelings in a melancholy conflict. He liked the cloth to be laid, for it had been the fashion of his youth, yet his conviction that heavy suppers were very unwholesome made him rather uneasy at seeing anything placed upon it; and while his hospitality would have welcomed his visitors to everything, his concern for their health caused him sorrow at the thought of them eating.

A small basin of thin gruel, like his own, was all he could, with thorough self‑approval, recommend; though he might restrain himself, while the ladies were comfortably clearing away the finer dishes, to say:

“Mrs. Bates, may I suggest you try one of these eggs? A very soft‑boiled egg is not unwholesome. Serle knows how to boil an egg better than anyone. I would not recommend an egg boiled by anyone else; but you need not be frightened, they are very small, you see—one of our little eggs will not hurt you. Miss Bates, let Emma give you a _little_ bit of tart—a _very_ little bit. Ours are all apple‑tarts. You need not fear unwholesome preserves here. I do not advise the custard. Mrs. Goddard, what say you to _half_ a glass of wine? A _small_ half‑glass, diluted with water? I do not think it could disagree with you.”

Emma permitted her father to speak—but she served her guests in a far more satisfactory manner, and on that particular evening took particular pleasure in seeing them depart contented. The happiness of Miss Smith matched her intentions exactly. Miss Woodhouse was such a great figure in Highbury that the prospect of the introduction had brought both anxiety and delight; yet the modest, grateful little girl left with a highly gratified spirit, delighted by the kindness with which Miss Woodhouse had treated her all evening, and at last even shook her hand!

After a few minutes of silence, John Knightley began:

“I have never seen a man try so hard to be agreeable as Mr. Elton. He works hard when it comes to ladies. With men he can be rational, but with women he tries every trick.”

“Mr. Elton’s manners aren’t perfect,” Emma replied, “but when someone wants to please, we should overlook faults, and we do. A man who does his best with limited ability will be better than one who is careless but superior. There is such good temper and goodwill in Mr. Elton that one cannot help valuing him.”

“Yes,” John said slyly, “he seems to have a lot of goodwill toward you.”

“Me!” she said, surprised, “are you thinking I am the object of Mr. Elton’s affection?”

Emma felt sorry for herself. She had to be polite to someone she didn’t like for three long months—always doing more than she wanted and less than she should. Why she disliked Jane Fairfax was hard to explain. Mr. Knightley had once said it was because Emma saw in Jane the truly accomplished young woman she wanted to be thought of herself. Emma had denied that at the time, but sometimes she wondered if there was some truth to it. She also thought Jane was always cold and distant, as if she didn’t care whether she was liked or not. On top of that, Emma’s aunt talked nonstop, and everyone fussed over Jane. People assumed the two girls, being the same age, must be close friends, which only added to Emma’s irritation. Those were the only reasons she could give.

Her dislike was small, but every imagined fault seemed huge in her mind. She never saw Jane after a long absence without feeling she had somehow offended her. When Jane finally visited after two years, Emma was struck by her appearance and manners—things Emma had been criticizing for the whole time. Jane was very elegant, perhaps the most elegant Emma had ever seen. She was of a height that most people would call tall, though not overly so, and her figure was graceful. Her size was a pleasant middle ground between plump and thin, though a slight hint of ill‑health suggested she might be prone to one of those conditions. Emma could not ignore all of this. Jane’s face was more beautiful than Emma remembered; it was not perfectly regular, but it was a very pleasing beauty. Her eyes were a deep grey, framed by dark lashes and eyebrows, and they had always earned praise. The skin Emma had once complained was too pale now had a clear, delicate quality that needed no extra color. This kind of beauty was defined by elegance, and Emma felt she had to admire it honestly, because elegance—whether of appearance or mind—was rare in Highbury. There, true distinction and merit were not vulgar.

In short, during Jane’s first visit, Emma watched her with a mixed feeling of pleasure and a sense of doing what was right. She decided she would try to stop disliking her. As she learned more about Jane’s background, her situation, and her beauty, and thought about what this elegance meant for Jane’s future—how she would live and what she might fall into—Emma could feel only compassion and respect. Especially when she added the likely possibility that Jane was attached to Mr. Dixon, a thought that seemed natural to her.

Mr. Elton’s importance to her grew slowly. At first she did not feel the same quick interest she had felt the day before, but as they talked she became more curious, amazed, and a little regretful. By the end of their conversation she imagined all the feelings—wonder, pain, pleasure—that might come from a fortunate Miss Hawkins, and she placed the Martins in a lower rank in her mind.

Emma was actually glad that the meeting had happened. It helped soften the initial shock without leaving any lasting alarm. Since Harriet was now living elsewhere, the Martins could not reach her unless they made the effort to seek her out—something they had never had the courage or the desire to do before. After she turned down the brother’s proposal, the sisters stopped visiting Mrs. Goddard’s, and a whole year could pass without any forced encounter or even a chance to speak.

Human nature tends to treat people in interesting situations with extra kindness; a young person who marries or dies is often spoken of warmly. Within a week of Miss Hawkins’s name first being mentioned in Highbury, everyone seemed to discover that she possessed every good quality—handsome, elegant, highly accomplished, and completely amiable. When Mr. Elton arrived, eager to share the news of her virtues, all he really needed to do was tell people her first name and mention the music she liked to play.

Mr. Elton returned a very happy man. He had left feeling rejected and humiliated after a hopeful courtship that seemed to have strong encouragement, only to lose the “right” lady and end up with someone he considered far less suitable. Yet he came back engaged to another woman—one who was, in his eyes, far superior to the first. He felt triumphant, self‑satisfied, and busy, caring little for Miss Woodhouse and ignoring Miss Smith.

The charming Augusta Hawkins, besides her usual beauty and merit, owned an independent fortune of about ten thousand pounds—a respectable sum that gave her both dignity and convenience. Mr. Elton felt he had not wasted his chance; he had secured a woman with a substantial dowry. Their courtship moved quickly: after a brief introduction, they were soon invited to dinner at Mr. Green’s and then to a party at Mrs. Brown’s. Smiles and blushes grew, and Augusta seemed easily impressed and very willing to accept him. In short, both vanity and prudence were satisfied with the rapid progress of their relationship.

He argued like a young man eager to dance, and Emma was surprised to see Mr. Weston’s easygoing nature clash so strongly with the Churchill family’s habits. He seemed to have all the energy, cheerfulness, and sociability of his father, and none of the pride or reserve of Enscombe. In fact, there was almost no pride at all; his casual attitude toward rank was almost rude. He could not judge the foolishness of his own cheap jokes—it was just a burst of lively spirit.

Finally, he was persuaded to move away from the front of the Crown. Now almost opposite the house where the Bateses lived, Emma remembered that he had planned to visit the day before and asked if he had done so.

“Yes, oh yes,” he replied. “I was just about to mention it. The visit went very well—I saw all three ladies and felt very grateful to you for your hint. If the talkative aunt had truly surprised me, it would have been the end of me. Instead, I was drawn into a very long visit. Ten minutes would have been enough, perhaps even proper; I told my father I would be home before him, but there was no way to leave, no pause. To my amazement, when he finally found me there, I realized I had been sitting with them for almost forty‑five minutes. The lady didn’t give me any chance to escape.

“And how did Miss Fairfax look?”

“Very ill—if a young lady can ever be called ill. But that phrase isn’t really appropriate, Mrs. Weston, is it? Ladies never look ill. Honestly, Miss Fairfax is naturally very pale, which often makes her seem unwell—a most unfortunate lack of colour.

Emma disagreed and defended Miss Fairfax’s complexion. “She was never radiant, but she never let herself look sickly. Her skin had a softness and delicacy that gave her face a special elegance.” He listened politely, admitted he had heard the same from others, but confessed that nothing could replace a healthy glow. A good complexion adds beauty to ordinary features, and when features are already fine, the effect is even better—though he need not try to describe it.

“Well,” said Emma, “there’s no arguing about taste. At least you like her, except for her complexion.”

He shook his head and laughed. “I can’t separate Miss Fairfax from her complexion.”

“Did you see her often at Weymouth? Were you often in the same social circles?”

At that moment they were reaching Ford’s, and he hurriedly exclaimed, “Ah! This must be the shop everyone visits every day, as my father tells me. He comes to Highbury himself six days a week and always has business at Ford’s.”

“No one loves home more than I do,” I said. “I’m practically a proverb for it at Maple Grove. Selina often tells me, when she’s heading to Bristol, ‘I really can’t get this girl to leave the house. I have to go alone, even though I hate being stuck in the barouche‑landau without a companion; but Augusta, with all her good will, would never go beyond the park fence.’ She says that a lot, yet I’m not for total seclusion. In fact, I think it’s harmful when people shut themselves off from society completely. It’s better to be involved in the world in a balanced way—neither too much nor too little. I understand your situation, Miss Woodhouse—(glancing at Mr. Woodhouse)—your father’s health must be a great obstacle. Why doesn’t he try Bath? He really should. Let me recommend Bath to you. I’m sure it would do Mr. Woodhouse good.”

“My father tried it several times before, but it didn’t help, and Mr. Perry—whom you probably know—doesn’t think it would be useful now.”

“Ah, that’s a real shame, because I can assure you, Miss Woodhouse, that the waters are wonderfully soothing. In my own time at Bath I saw many examples of that! It’s such a cheerful place that it would surely lift Mr. Woodhouse’s spirits, which I hear are often low. As for you, the benefits of Bath for young people are well known. It would be a wonderful introduction for someone who has lived so a secluded life. I could instantly introduce you to the best society there. A word from me would bring you a small circle of acquaintances, and my close friend Mrs. Partridge—the lady I always stay with when I’m in Bath—would be delighted to look after you and would be the perfect person to take you out in public.”

Emma could only tolerate so much before it became impolite. The thought of owing Mrs. Elton an “introduction”—being taken into society under the patronage of a friend of Mrs. Elton’s, probably some flashy, newly‑wed widow who lives off a boarder—was mortifying. The dignity of Miss Woodhouse of Hartfield was truly damaged.

She held back any sharp rebuke she might have made and thanked Mrs. Elton politely, “but going to Bath is completely out of the question; I’m not convinced the place would suit me better than my father.” To avoid further offense, she quickly changed the subject.

“I’m not asking whether you are musical, Mrs. Elton. In these situations a lady’s reputation usually comes first, and Highbury has long known you to be an excellent performer.”

“The amount of your admiration might surprise you someday,” said Emma.

Mr. Knightley was busy fastening the lower buttons of his thick leather gaiters. The effort, or perhaps something else, flushed his face as he replied, “Oh! Are you there?—But you are terribly late. Mr. Cole hinted at it to me six weeks ago.” He paused. Emma felt Mrs. Weston press her foot against hers and was unsure what to think. A moment later he continued, “That will never happen, I assure you. Miss Fairfax would not accept me even if I asked, and I am certain I will never ask her.”

Emma pressed her foot back, interested, and exclaimed, “You are not vain, Mr. Knightley. I will say that for you.” He seemed barely to hear her, lost in thought, and, looking displeased, said, “So you have been arranging for me to marry Jane Fairfax?”

“No, I have not,” Emma replied quickly. “You have scolded me enough about matchmaking that I would never presume to speak for you. What I said just now meant nothing. People say such things without any real intention. I swear I have no desire at all for you to marry Jane Fairfax—or anyone else. You would not sit with us so comfortably if you were married.”

Mr. Knightley fell silent again. At last he said, “No, Emma, I do not think my admiration for her will ever surprise me. I have never thought of her that way, I assure you.” He added, “Jane Fairfax is a very charming young woman, but she is not perfect. She lacks the open temperament a man would want in a wife.”

Emma was glad to hear that she had a fault. “Well,” she said, “and you have already silenced Mr. Cole, I suppose?”

“Yes, very quickly. He gave me a gentle hint; I told him he was wrong, he apologized and said nothing more. Mr. Cole does not try to be wiser or wittier than his neighbours.”

“In that respect he is nothing like dear Mrs. Elton, who wants to be wiser and wittier than everyone! I wonder how she talks about the Coles—what nickname she uses for them! She calls you ‘Knightley’—what can she do for Mr. Cole? No wonder Jane Fairfax accepts her politeness and agrees to be with her. Mrs. Weston, your argument convinces me. I can more easily imagine leaving Miss Bates than believing Miss Fairfax’s mind will triumph over Mrs. Elton’s. I have no faith that Mrs. Elton will admit she is inferior in thought, speech, or deed, or that she is held back by any real sense of good breeding. I cannot imagine she will stop flattering her guests with praise, encouragement, and offers of service, or stop describing her grand plans—whether securing a permanent position for her or inviting her to the delightful outings in the carriage‑landau.”

I was hurrying along, just after crossing a ditch I knew was close to the Battery, and I had just scrambled up the mound beyond it when I saw a man sitting in front of me. His back was to me, his arms folded, and he was nodding forward, heavy with sleep.

I thought he’d appreciate a surprise breakfast, so I stepped forward quietly and touched his shoulder. He jumped up instantly, and it wasn’t the same man at all—it was another one!

This new man was also dressed in coarse gray, had a big iron on his leg, was lame, hoarse, cold—everything the first man was, except his face was different and he wore a flat, broad‑brimmed, low‑crowned felt hat. I only had a split second to notice it; he swore at me, swung a weak punch that missed and almost knocked himself down, then fled into the mist, stumbling twice as he went, and I lost sight of him.

“It’s the young man!” I thought, my heart leaping as I recognized him. I’m sure I would have felt a pain in my liver too, if I’d known where it was.

I soon reached the Battery, and there was the right man—hugging himself and limping back and forth, as if he hadn’t stopped hugging and limping all night—waiting for me. He was terribly cold, indeed. I half expected him to collapse in front of me and die of the cold. His eyes looked so hungry that when I handed him the file and he set it on the grass, I thought he might have tried to eat it if he hadn’t seen my bundle. This time he didn’t flip me over to get at what I was carrying; he left me upright while I opened the bundle and emptied my pockets.

“What’s in the bottle, boy?” he asked.

“Brandy,” I replied.

He was already shoveling minced meat down his throat in a strange way—more like someone stuffing it away in a frantic hurry than actually eating it—but he paused to take a sip of the liquor. He shivered so violently that he could barely keep the bottle’s neck between his teeth without biting it off.

“I think you’ve got the ague,” I said.

“I agree with you, boy,” he replied.

“It’s bad out here,” I told him. “You’ve been lying on the meshes, and they’re terribly fever‑ish. Rheumatic too.”

“I’ll eat my breakfast before they kill me,” he said. “I’d do that if I were about to be hanged on that gallows over there right after. I’ll shake these shivers off, I’ll bet you.”

He was gobbling minced meat, meatbone, bread, cheese, and pork pie all at once, glancing distrustfully at the mist surrounding us, often stopping—sometimes even stopping his jaws—to listen.

I leaned over Joe and, using my finger, read the whole letter to him.

"Amazing!" Joe said when I finished. "You really are a scholar."

"How do you spell Gargery, Joe?" I asked, trying to be helpful.

"I don't know how to spell it at all," Joe replied.

"What if you did?"

"It can't be supposed," he said. "Even though I love reading, I'm not good at spelling."

"Do you love reading, Joe?"

"Very much. Give me a good book or a good newspaper, sit me by a warm fire, and I couldn't ask for more. Lord, when you finally get a J and an O and say, 'Here, at last, is a J‑O, Joe,' reading becomes fascinating!"

I realized that Joe's education, like a steam engine, was still in its early stages. I pressed on:

"Did you ever go to school when you were as little as I was?"

"No, Pip."

"Why not?"

Joe picked up the poker and settled into his usual habit of slowly raking the fire between the lower bars. "I'll tell you. My father was a drunk. When he got drunk he would beat my mother mercilessly. That was almost the only beating he gave anyone else, except me. He beat me with a vigor that could only be matched by the vigor with which he didn't beat his own will. Are you listening, Pip?"

"Yes, Joe."

"Because of that, my mother and I ran away from him many times. She would go to work and say, 'Joe, now, please God, you shall have some schooling, child,' and she would try to send me to school. But my father, though he had a good heart, couldn't bear to be without us. He would come with a terrible crowd and make such a racket at the doors of the houses where we stayed that the owners were forced to give us up to him. He would take us home and beat us. You see, Pip, that stopped me from learning."

"Poor Joe!" I said sympathetically.

"But mind you, Pip," Joe added, tapping the top bar of the poker a couple of times, "my father, despite everything, was good at heart, you see?"

I didn't quite understand, but I said nothing.

"Well!" Joe continued, "someone has to keep the pot boiling, Pip, or the pot won't boil, you know?"

I nodded.

"Since my father didn't object to me working, I took a job that was the same as his would have been if he had followed it. I worked hard, Pip, I assure you. Over time I was able to support him, and I kept him until he died in a sudden fit. I wanted to put on his tombstone something like, 'Whatever his faults, remember he was good at heart.'"

“You never say anything about her,” Miss Havisham said, watching me. “She says many harsh things about you, but you say nothing about her. What do you think of her?”

“I don’t know how to say it,” I stammered.

“Tell me quietly,” she said, leaning down.

“I think she is very proud,” I whispered.

“Anything else?”

“She is very pretty.”

“Anything else?”

“She is very insulting.” (She looked at me with complete disgust.)

“Anything else?”

“I would like to go home.”

“And never see her again, even though she’s so pretty?”

“I’m not sure I don’t want to see her again, but I do want to go home now.”

“You will go soon,” Miss Havisham said aloud. “Finish the game.”

Except for the odd smile at the start, I was almost certain Miss Havisham could not smile at all. Her face was fixed in a watchful, brooding look, as if everything about her had become frozen, and nothing could lift it again. She hunched her shoulders, and her voice dropped low, sounding dead and lullaby‑like; she seemed to have both body and soul pressed down by a crushing weight.

I played the game to the end with Estella, and she ruined me. She threw the cards down on the table when she had won them all, as if she despised the fact that she had taken them from me.

“When shall I have you here again?” Miss Havisham asked. “Let me think.”

I began to remind her that today was Wednesday, when she snapped at me with the impatient flick of her right hand.

“There, there! I don’t know the days of the week; I don’t know the weeks of the year. Come back in six days. Understand?”

“Yes, ma’am.”

“Estella, take him down. Let him have something to eat, and let him walk around while he eats. Go, Pip.”

I followed the candle down, just as I had followed it up, and she placed it where we had found it. Until she opened the side door, I had imagined, without thinking, that it must be night. The sudden rush of daylight confused me, making me feel as if I had been in that candle‑lit room for many hours.

“You wait here, boy,” Estella said, then disappeared and closed the door.

Alone in the courtyard, I looked at my rough hands and plain boots. I didn’t like how they looked now; they seemed vulgar. I thought about asking Joe why he ever taught me to call those picture cards Jacks, when they should be called knaves. I wished Joe had been brought up more genteel, so I might have been, too.

She returned with some bread, meat, and a small mug of beer. She set the mug on the stone floor and handed me the bread and meat without looking at me, as insolently as if I were a disgraced dog.

“Well, miss?” I answered, almost tripping over her and catching myself.

She stared at me, and I stared back.

“Am I pretty?”

“Yes; I think you are very pretty.”

“Am I insulting?”

“Not as much as you were last time,” I said.

“Not as much as?”

“No.”

She snapped when I asked the last question, and she slapped my face hard as she answered.

“Now?” she demanded. “You little coarse monster, what do you think of me now?”

“I won’t tell you.”

“Because you’ll tell upstairs. Is that it?”

“No,” I replied, “that’s not it.”

“Why don’t you cry again, you little wretch?”

“Because I’ll never cry for you again,” I said. That was probably as false a promise as any; inside I was actually crying for her, and I knew the pain she would later cause me.

We went upstairs after that argument, and while we were climbing we met a man feeling his way down.

“Who have we here?” the man asked, stopping to look at me.

“A boy,” Estella answered.

He was a big, dark‑skinned man with a huge head and an equally large hand. He lifted my chin with that hand and looked at me in the candlelight. He was bald on top, had thick black eyebrows that stuck up, deep‑set sharp eyes, a big watch chain, and black spots where a beard would have been. He meant nothing to me then, and I had no idea he would ever matter, but I got a good look at him.

“Neighbourhood boy? Hey?” he said.

“Yes, sir,” I replied.

“How did you get here?”

“Miss Havisham sent for me, sir,” I explained.

“Alright! Behave yourself. I’ve dealt with many boys, and you’re a bad lot. Now mind!” he said, biting his forefinger and frowning at me, “you behave yourself!”

With that, he let go of me—his hand smelled of scented soap, which I welcomed—and walked down. I wondered if he might be a doctor, but no; a doctor would have been calmer and more persuasive. There was no time to think, because we soon entered Miss Havisham’s room, where everything was just as I had left it. Estella left me standing by the door, and I waited until Miss Havisham looked up from the dressing table.

“So!” she said, without surprise: “the days have worn away, have they?”

“Yes, ma’am. Today is—”

“There, there, there!” she snapped, waving her fingers impatiently. “I don’t want to know. Are you ready to play?”

I answered, a little confused, “I don’t think I am, ma’am.”

Then he and my sister would get into these ridiculous speculations about Miss Havisham and what she might do for me, that I often felt like bursting into angry tears and lashing out at Pumblechook. In those conversations my sister talked to me as if she were pulling a tooth out of my mouth with every mention, while Pumblechook—who had appointed himself my patron—watched me with a contemptuous eye, like a director of my fate who thought his job was unrewarding.

Joe never took part in those talks. Still, they talked about him while they were going on, because Mrs. Joe sensed he wasn’t keen on me leaving the forge. I was old enough now to be Joe’s apprentice, and when Joe sat with the poker on his knees, carefully raking the ashes from the lower bars, my sister would twist that innocent action into opposition, jump at him, snatch the poker from his hands, shake him, and put it away. Each of those debates ended in the most irritating way. In an instant, with no warning, my sister would yawn, glance at me as if by accident, and say, “Come on! That’s enough of you! You go to bed; you’ve caused enough trouble for one night, I hope!” as if I had asked them as a favor to ruin my life.

We kept going like that for a long time, and it seemed likely we’d keep it up for a while, when one day Miss Havisham stopped short while we were walking, leaning on my shoulder, and said, a little annoyed, “You’re getting tall, Pip!” I tried to hint with a thoughtful look that it was something beyond my control.

She didn’t say anything else then, but she kept stopping, looking at me again, and again, then frowning. The next day, after our usual walk, when I had helped her to her dressing table, she held up her impatient fingers and said, “Tell me again the name of that blacksmith of yours.”

“Joe Gargery, ma’am.”

“Do you mean the master you’re supposed to be apprenticed to?”

“Yes, Miss Havisham.”

“You’d better start the apprenticeship right away. Do you think Gargery will come here with you and bring your indenture?”

I indicated that I was sure he’d be honored to be asked.

“Then let him come.”

“At what time, Miss Havisham?”

“There, there! I’m not worried about the timing. Let him come soon, and come with you.”

When I got home that night and delivered the message to Joe, my sister “went on a rampage,” more dramatically than ever before. She asked Joe and me if we thought she was a doormat under our feet, how we could treat her that way, and what sort of company she was supposedly fit for.

Then my sister and I would sit and argue about Miss Havisham, guessing what she might do for me. I often felt like crying in spite, wanting to fly at Pumblechook and beat him. In those talks my sister seemed to pull at my heart like she was pulling a tooth out each time Miss Havisham was mentioned. Pumblechook, who thought of himself as my patron, watched me with a disapproving eye, as if he were the architect of my future on a very unrewarding job.

Joe never joined those conversations, but they talked about him while they were going on because Mrs. Joe thought he didn’t want me taken away from the forge. I was old enough now to be Joe’s apprentice, and when Joe sat with a poker on his knees, slowly shoveling ash from the lower bars, my sister would twist that innocent act into opposition. She would rush over, snatch the poker from his hands, shake him, and put the poker away. Every debate ended the same way: without any warning my sister would yawn, glance at me, and say, “Come! That’s enough of you! You go to bed; you’ve caused enough trouble for one night, I hope!” as if I had asked them as a favor to bother my life.

We kept doing this for a long time, and it seemed we would continue forever, when one day Miss Havisham stopped while we were walking, leaning on my shoulder, and said, a little annoyed, “You’re getting tall, Pip!” I tried to hint with a thoughtful look that this was something beyond my control.

She said nothing more at the moment, but she kept looking at me, again and again, her face growing frowning and moody. The next day, after our usual walk, I helped her settle at her dressing table. She stopped me with an impatient finger and asked, “Tell me again the name of that blacksmith of yours.”

“Joe Gargery, ma’am.”

“Do you mean the master you’re supposed to be apprenticed to?”

“Yes, Miss Havisham.”

“You’d better start your apprenticeship at once. Do you think Gargery will come here with you and bring your indenture papers?”

I indicated that I was sure he would be honored to be asked.

“Then let him come.”

“At what time, Miss Havisham?”

“There, there! I don’t know about times. Let him come soon, and bring you along.”

When I got home that night and gave Joe the message, my sister “went on the rampage,” more wildly than ever before. She shouted at both me and Joe, asking if we thought she was a doormat under our feet, how we could treat her that way, and what sort of company we thought she was fit for.

“Good. You’d better go to his house. The way will be ready for you, and you can see his son first, who is in London. When will you come to London?”

I looked at Joe, who was standing still, and said I thought I could go straight there.

“First,” said Mr. Jaggers, “you’ll need some decent clothes, not work‑clothes. Give yourself a week to get them. You’ll also need money. Shall I give you twenty guineas?”

He took a long purse from his pocket, counted the money on the table, and pushed it toward me. It was the first time he moved from his chair. He sat on the edge of the chair, swung the purse, and stared at Joe.

“Joseph Gargery, you look stunned,” he said.

“I am!” Joe replied firmly.

“It was agreed you wanted nothing for yourself, remember?” Jaggers asked.

“Yes, that was agreed,” Joe said. “And it will stay that way.”

“But what if my instructions were to give you a gift as compensation?” Jaggers continued, swinging the purse.

“For what compensation?” Joe asked.

“For the loss of his services.”

Joe placed his hand on my shoulder with a gentle touch. I have often thought of him since as a strong man who can also be gentle, like a steam‑hammer that can crush a man or tap an egg‑shell. “Pip,” Joe said, “you are welcome to go free with his services, with honor and good fortune, as words cannot fully express. But if you think money can replace the loss of the little boy—what comes to the forge—and the best of friends!”

Oh, good Joe, whom I was ready to leave and had not thanked, I see you again, with your strong blacksmith’s arm, your broad chest rising, and your voice fading. Dear, faithful Joe, I feel the tremor of your hand on my arm, as solemn today as an angel’s wing.

I encouraged Joe then. I was lost in thoughts of my future fortunes and could not remember the paths we had walked together. I begged Joe to be comforted, because, as he said, we had always been the best of friends, and as I said, we always would be. Joe wiped his eyes with his wrist, as if trying to erase them, but said nothing more.

Mr. Jaggers watched this, seeing Joe as a simple country man and me as his guardian. When the moment passed, he weighed the purse in his hand and said:

“Now, Joseph Gargery, this is your last chance. No half‑measures with me. If you want the gift I’m supposed to give you, say so and you’ll have it. If, on the contrary, you intend to refuse—”

At that moment Joe suddenly lunged at him, showing a fierce, fighting stance.

Mr. Pumblechook rose again and said, "I cannot look at One and drink to One without asking—may I?" I told him he could, and we shook hands, emptied our glasses, and turned them upside down. I did the same; if I had turned myself upside down before drinking, the wine would have gone straight to my head.

He helped me onto the liver wing and the best slice of tongue, taking no care of himself at all. "Ah, poultry!" he said, addressing the bird on the plate. "When you were a young chick, you never imagined you'd end up as food under this humble roof for someone weak. May I?" He repeated the request immediately, as if it were a habit, and I wondered how he could do it so often without hurting himself with my knife.

After a few bites, he turned to my sister, who had raised me. "It's sad," he said, "that she can no longer fully understand the honor she gave you. May—" I saw he was about to say more and stopped him. "We'll drink to her health," I said.

Mr. Pumblechook leaned back, admiringly flattered, and exclaimed, "That's the way you know them, sir!" He set his untouched glass down quickly, rose again, and repeated his polite request, "May I?" He then sat down, raised his glass to my sister, and said, "Let us never be blind to her temper, but hope she meant well."

At that moment I noticed his face flushing, and I felt my own cheeks burn from the wine. I told Mr. Pumblechook that I wanted my new clothes sent to his house. He was delighted at the thought of being trusted with them. I explained that I wished to avoid being seen in the village, and he praised the idea, saying that no one but himself was worthy of my confidence. He asked me tenderly if I remembered our boyhood games, how we had gone together to arrange my apprenticeship, and how he had always been my favorite friend. If I had drunk ten more glasses, I might have realized that he never truly saw me that way and would have rejected the notion. Yet, despite all that, I felt convinced that I had been wrong about him and that he was a sensible, practical, good‑hearted man.

I then learned that Wemmick was the clerk in the next room. While he was away, another clerk was called down from upstairs to take his place, and after shaking hands with my guardian I went with him onto the street. A new crowd was lingering outside, but Wemmick pushed through them, saying coolly but firmly, "I tell you it’s no use; he won’t have a word to say to any of you," and we soon got past them and walked side by side.

Chapter XXI.

Looking at Mr. Wemmick as we walked, I saw what he looked like in daylight. He was a short, dry‑looking man with a square, wooden‑like face that seemed carved with a blunt chisel. The chisel had left a few shallow dents where it tried to make dimples, especially around his nose, but never smoothed them out. His linen was frayed, so I guessed he was a bachelor, and he wore at least four mourning rings, a brooch shaped like a lady, and a small weeping‑willow tomb with an urn. Several rings and seals hung from his watch chain, as if he carried many reminders of dead friends. His eyes were small, sharp, and black; his lips were thin, wide, and mottled. I thought he must have been in his forties or fifties.

"So you’ve never been to London before?" Mr. Wemmick asked.

"No," I replied.

"I was new here once, too," he said. "Hard to think about now!"

"Do you know it well now?"

"Yes," he answered. "I know the ways of it."

"Is it a very wicked place?" I asked, more to keep the conversation going than out of real curiosity.

"You can be cheated, robbed, even murdered in London. But there are plenty of people everywhere who will do those things for you."

"What if you have a bad feeling about them?" I tried to soften the question.

"Oh, I don’t know about bad feelings," he said. "There isn’t much of that. They’ll do it if there’s something to gain."

"That makes it worse," I said.

"You think so?" he replied. "It’s about the same, I’d say."

He wore his hat pushed back on his head and stared straight ahead, walking as if nothing in the street could distract him. His mouth looked like a post‑office box, giving a mechanical smile. When we reached the top of Holborn Hill I realized his smile was only a habit; he wasn’t really smiling at all.

"Do you know where Mr. Matthew Pocket lives?" I asked.

"Yes," he said, nodding toward the direction. "In Hammersmith, west of London."

"Is that far?"

“Also to Ceylon, especially for elephant tusks.”

“You’ll need a lot of ships,” I said.

“A whole fleet,” he answered.

Impressed by the scale of his plans, I asked where the ships he intended to insure would be sailing now.

“I haven’t started insuring yet,” he said. “I’m just looking around.”

That answer sounded more like something you’d hear at Barnard’s Inn. I replied confidently, “Ah‑h!”

“Yes. I work in a counting‑house and I’m watching what’s happening.”

“Is a counting‑house a good way to make money?” I asked.

“To—do you mean the young man who works there?” he asked back.

“Yes, to you.”

“Not really. It doesn’t pay me directly, and I have to support myself.” He said it as if he were carefully adding up numbers on a ledger.

It didn’t sound profitable, and I shook my head, thinking it would be hard to save any capital from such a job.

“But the point,” said Herbert Pocket, “is that you keep looking around. That’s the important part. You’re in a counting‑house, you know, and you keep observing.”

It seemed odd to me that you could not leave a counting‑house and still look around, but I trusted his experience.

“Then the time will come,” Herbert continued, “when you see an opening. You jump on it, make your capital, and that’s it. Once you have your capital, all you have to do is use it.”

His words reminded me of the way he behaved in the garden—calm and steady. The way he carried his poverty matched the way he handled defeat. He took every setback with the same calm attitude I had seen before. It was clear he owned only the basics; everything else I noticed had been sent to him from the coffee‑house or elsewhere.

Even though he imagined himself already rich, he stayed modest, and I was grateful he didn’t become arrogant. His natural kindness made our friendship easy. In the evening we walked through the streets, got half‑price tickets to the theatre, and the next day we went to Westminster Abbey for service. In the afternoon we strolled in the parks, and I wondered who shod all the horses there, hoping it was Joe.

It had been many months—several Sundays—since I left Joe and Biddy. The distance between us grew, and the marshes where we lived seemed far away. The thought of returning to our old church in my old Sunday clothes on the very last Sunday ever felt impossible, both geographically and socially, like the sun and moon could not meet. Yet the crowded London streets, bright in the dusk, reminded me of the guilt I felt for leaving the poor kitchen at home. In the dead of night, the footsteps of some useless porter pretending to watch Barnard’s Inn echoed hollowly in my heart.

“Who’s the Spider?”

“The spider?” I answered.

“The blotchy, sprawling, sulky fellow.”

“That’s Bentley Drummle,” I said; “the one with the delicate face is Startop.”

Without giving any heed to “the one with the delicate face,” he replied, “Bentley Drummle is his name, is it? I like the look of that fellow.”

He instantly turned his attention to Drummle, undeterred by my terse reply, and seemed to press him into conversation. I was watching the two when the housekeeper entered, bearing the first dish for the table.

She seemed about forty, though I may have thought her younger. She was rather tall, lithe and nimble, extremely pale, with large faded eyes and a mass of streaming hair. I could not tell whether some heart ailment made her lips perpetually slightly open, as if she were breathing hard, and gave her face a strange, sudden, fluttering expression; but I remembered having seen Macbeth at the theatre a night or two before, and her face struck me as if it were all disturbed by a fiery wind, like the faces that rise from the witches’ cauldron.

I covered my face with my hands and peered through the dark windows—opening them even a little was impossible in that wind and rain—and saw that the courtyard lamps were out, the lamps on the bridges and shore were flickering, and the coal fires on barges in the river were being blown out like red‑hot splashes in the rain.

I read with my watch on the table, planning to close my book at eleven o’clock. As I shut it, Saint Paul’s and the many church clocks in the city began to strike the hour. The wind made the sound sound strange, and I was listening, thinking about how the wind battered and tore at it, when I heard a footstep on the stairs.

I don’t know why I jumped, thinking of my dead sister’s footstep, but the sound faded quickly. I listened again and heard the footstep coming up, stumbling. Remembering that the stair lamps were out, I took my reading lamp and went to the top of the stairs. Whoever was below stopped when they saw my lamp, and everything was quiet.

"Is there someone down there?" I called, looking down.

"Yes," a voice answered from the darkness.

"Which floor do you want?"

"The top. Mr. Pip."

"That’s my name—what’s the matter?"

"Nothing," the voice replied, and the man kept coming up.

In draughts, on the other hand, the moves are limited and similar, so accidental errors are rarer, and the little attention that is left unused means that any advantage comes from superior insight.

To glance at a star sideways—viewing it with the outer parts of the retina, which are more prone to faint light impressions than the inner—gives a distinct view, the best appreciation of its brilliance—a brilliance that dims precisely as we stare at it directly. More rays strike the eye in the latter case, but the former offers a finer capacity for understanding. Excessive profundity confounds and weakens thought; one can even make Venus disappear from the heavens by looking too long, too intensely, or too directly.

“We mean you no harm at all. I promise you, as a gentleman and as a Frenchman, that we do not intend to hurt you. I know you are innocent of the murders in the Rue Morgue, but you are still involved in some way. As I have already explained, I have information about this case that you could never have imagined. The sailor had mostly regained his composure while Dupin spoke, but his earlier confidence had vanished.

“So help me God!” he said after a short pause. “I will tell you everything I know about this case; but I do not expect you to believe half of what I say—I would be a fool to think otherwise. Still, I am innocent, and I will keep my word even if I die for it.”

He then gave his story. He had recently taken a voyage to the Indonesian islands. A group he was part of landed in Borneo and went on a pleasure trip inland. He and a companion captured an orang‑utan. The companion died, leaving the animal in his sole possession. After much difficulty—because the animal was extremely fierce during the trip back home—he finally managed to bring it safely to his home in Paris. To avoid attracting unwanted attention from his neighbors, he kept the animal hidden until it healed from a foot wound caused by a splinter on the ship. He planned to sell it.

One morning, after a night of sailors’ revelry, he returned home and found the beast in his own bedroom. It had escaped from a nearby closet where it had been thought to be securely locked. The orang‑utan was holding a razor, fully lathered, standing before a mirror, apparently trying to shave after having watched its master through the closet’s keyhole. Terrified by the sight of such a dangerous weapon in the hands of a ferocious animal, the man was momentarily unsure what to do. He was used to calming the creature, even when it was angry, with a whip, so he tried that again. As soon as he saw the animal, the orang‑utan leapt out of the room, down the stairs, and out through an open window onto the street.

The Frenchman chased after it in desperation; the ape, still holding the razor, occasionally stopped to look back and gesture at its pursuer, until the man almost caught up with it.

Nobody went to see the body. Nothing was said or heard about it in the Rue Pavée St. Andrée, even by the people who lived in the same building. M. St. Eustache, who loved Marie and was going to marry her, lived in her mother’s house. He says he did not learn that a body had been found until the next morning, when M. Beauvais entered his room and told him. For a piece of news like that, it is striking that he says he heard it so calmly.

The newspaper tried to make it look as if Marie’s relatives didn’t care, which would contradict the idea that they thought the corpse was hers. The paper hinted that Marie, with the help of her friends, had left the city for a reason that might damage her reputation, and that those friends, when a body that looked like hers was found in the Seine, used the chance to convince the public that she was dead. But L’Etoile was too quick to judge. It was clearly shown that there was no such indifference. The old lady was very weak and so upset that she could not perform any duties. St. Eustache was not calm at all; he was distraught and behaved so wildly that M. Beauvais had to get a friend and a relative to look after him and stop him from attending the examination of the body.

To add some color to the suspicion against Beauvais, a visitor to his office a few days before the girl disappeared, while Beauvais was away, saw a rose placed in the key‑hole of the door and a slate nearby with the name “Marie” written on it.

To me, this article seems to amount to little more than the enthusiasm of its writer. We must remember that, in general, newspapers aim more at creating a sensation—to make a point—than at advancing truth. The latter is only pursued when it coincides with the former. Print that merely aligns with common opinion (no matter how well‑founded that opinion may be) gains no favor with the crowd. The masses consider only the one who offers _sharp contradictions_ of the prevailing view to be profound. In reasoning, as in literature, the epigram is the most instantly and universally admired. In both fields it ranks at the lowest level of merit.

"What I intend to say is that it is the mixture of epigram and melodrama surrounding the notion that Marie Rogêt still lives—rather than any genuine plausibility in the idea—that prompted L’Etoile to publish it and earned it a warm reception from the public. Let us examine the headings of this journal’s argument, trying to avoid the incoherence with which it was originally presented."

"The writer’s first goal is to demonstrate, by the short span between Marie’s disappearance and the discovery of the floating corpse, that the corpse could not be Marie’s. Shrinking this interval to its smallest possible length becomes, at once, the object of the reasoner’s attention. In his hasty chase after this object, he leaps to mere conjecture at the outset. ‘It is folly to suppose,’ he says, ‘that the murder—if a murder was indeed committed on her body—could have been completed quickly enough for the killers to cast the body into the river before midnight.’ We naturally ask, why? Why is it folly to suppose the murder occurred _within five minutes_ after the girl left her mother’s house? Why is it folly to suppose the murder happened at any particular time of day? Assassinations have occurred at all hours. Yet, had the murder taken place at any moment between nine o’clock on Sunday morning and a quarter to midnight, there would still have been sufficient time ‘to throw the body into the river before midnight.’ This assumption therefore amounts precisely to the claim—that the murder did not happen on Sunday at all—and, if we allow L’Etoile to make this claim, we may grant it any liberty. Because they felt a deep responsibility toward the creature they had created, and because they were full of tenderness, I can imagine that during every hour of my early life I learned patience, charity, and self‑control. I was guided by a gentle thread that made everything seem like one continuous pleasure.

For a long time I was their only concern. My mother had always wanted a daughter, but I remained their only child. When I was about five, they took a trip beyond Italy’s borders and spent a week on the shores of Lake Como. Their kind nature often led them to visit the cottages of the poor. For my mother this was more than a duty; it was a passion—she remembered how she had once suffered and been helped, and now she wanted to be the guardian angel for those in need. During one of their walks they noticed a shabby hut in a valley that looked especially sad, and a group of half‑clothed children gathered around showed how deep the poverty was.

One day, while my father was away in Milan, my mother took me to see the hut. Inside they found a peasant couple, exhausted by work, giving a meager meal to five hungry babies. One of the children caught my mother’s eye more than the others. The other four were dark‑eyed, tough little wanderers; this child was thin and very fair. Her hair shone like bright gold, and even though her clothes were poor, it seemed to crown her head. Her forehead was smooth and wide, her blue eyes clear, and her lips and face were so expressive of feeling and sweetness that anyone who saw her would think she belonged to a different, almost heavenly, kind.

Seeing my mother stare in wonder, the peasant woman quickly told her the girl’s story. She was not the couple’s own child but the daughter of a Milanese nobleman. Her mother had been German and died giving birth. The baby had been left with these good people to be nursed; they were better off then. The couple had not been married long, and their first child had just been born. The girl’s father was one of those Italians who dreamed of Italy’s ancient glory—a member of the “still‑shouting slaves” who fought for their country’s freedom. He became a victim of its weakness. Whether he was dead or still imprisoned in Austria was unknown. His property was taken away; his daughter became an orphan and a beggar. She stayed with her foster parents and grew in their rough home, brighter than a garden rose among dark brambles.

When my father came back from Milan, he found in the hall of our villa a child more beautiful than a painted cherub—a being whose looks seemed to radiate light and whose movements were as light as a mountain goat.

How much has already been accomplished, declared the spirit within Frankenstein—yet I shall accomplish even more; following the paths already traced, I shall blaze a new trail, probe unseen forces, and reveal to mankind the profound secrets of creation.

I did not close my eyes that night. My inner self was in a state of rebellion and unrest; I sensed that order would eventually emerge, though I lacked the power to bring it about. Gradually, as dawn broke, sleep finally came. When I awoke, the thoughts of the previous night seemed like a fleeting dream. All that remained was a determination to return to my old studies and devote myself to a science for which I felt a natural aptitude. That same day I called on M. Waldman. In private his manners were even gentler and more appealing than in public; the dignity he displayed during his lecture gave way, at home, to a great warmth and kindness. I gave him almost the same account of my former pursuits that I had given to his colleague. He listened attentively to the brief narration of my studies and smiled at the names Cornelius Agrippa and Paracelsus, but without the scorn that M. Krempe had shown. He remarked, “These were men whose tireless zeal provided modern philosophers with much of the foundation of their knowledge. They left us a simpler task: to assign new names and arrange the facts they uncovered into coherent classifications. Even when the efforts of brilliant men are misdirected, they rarely fail to ultimately benefit humanity.” I heard his words, spoken without pretension, and then told him that his lecture had dispelled my prejudice against contemporary chemists; I expressed myself with measured modesty and the deference a young student owes his teacher, while allowing the enthusiasm that drove my intended work to shine through. I asked for his guidance on which books I should obtain.

“I am pleased,” said M. Waldman, “to have found a disciple; and if your diligence matches your talent, I have no doubt of your success. Chemistry is the branch of natural philosophy where the greatest advances have been made and where further improvements are still possible; that is why I have devoted myself to it.
